name: Amaziah (son of Joash)
title: King of Judah who defeated Edom but fell into pride
summary: Amaziah, son of King Joash and Joadan from Jerusalem, took the throne of Judah at age 25 and reigned for 29 years (ca. 796–767 B.C.). He began his reign by doing what was right in the Lord's sight, but not with a whole heart. After executing his father's murderers – yet sparing their children in accordance with the Law of Moses – he prepared for war against Edom. He hired one hundred thousand Israelite soldiers, but sent them back after a man of God warned him, which resulted in those rejected soldiers plundering cities of Judah. In the Valley of Salt, Amaziah won a decisive victory: ten thousand Edomites fell, and another ten thousand were taken captive. He captured the fortress city of Sela and renamed it Joktheel. The triumph, however, marked the beginning of his downfall. He brought Edomite idols to Jerusalem and began to worship them; when a prophet confronted him, he rejected the warning with threats. Drunk on military success, he challenged Joash king of Israel, who answered with a fable about a thistle on Lebanon that haughtily sent word to a cedar – only to be trampled by a wild beast. At Beth-Shemesh, Judah suffered a humiliating defeat: Amaziah was taken captive, Jerusalem's wall was torn down for 400 cubits, and the treasures of the temple and palace were carried off. Amaziah's final years were marked by weakened authority, and eventually a conspiracy was plotted against him. He fled to Lachish but was overtaken and killed. His son Azariah, also known as Uzziah, succeeded him.

keyEvents.title: Becomes king of Judah
keyEvents.description: Amaziah became king at the age of twenty-five and reigned for twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. He did what was right in the Lord's eyes, but not with a whole heart.

keyEvents.title: Punishes his father's murderers
keyEvents.description: When the kingdom was firmly established in his hands, he executed the servants who had killed his father King Joash, but spared their children in accordance with what is written in the Law of Moses.

keyEvents.title: Rejects Israeli mercenaries
keyEvents.description: Amaziah mustered the army of Judah and hired an additional hundred thousand Israelite soldiers. A man of God warned him against using them, and Amaziah sent them home despite the financial loss. The dismissed soldiers then plundered cities in Judah on their way back.

keyEvents.title: Victory over Edom in the Valley of Salt
keyEvents.description: Amaziah leded Judah's army to the Valley of Salt and defeated the Edomites. Ten thousand fell in battle, and another ten thousand were taken alive, thrown from a cliff. He also captured the city of Sela and renamed it Joktheel.

keyEvents.title: Worship of Edomite gods
keyEvents.description: After defeating Edom, Amaziah brought back the gods of the Edomites and bowed down to them. A prophet confronted him, but Amaziah rejected the warning and threatened the prophet.

keyEvents.title: Defeat by King Joash of Israel
keyEvents.description: In his pride, Amaziah challenged King Joash of Israel to war. Joash replied with a fable about a thistle on Lebanon that haughtily sent word to a cedar, asking it to give its daughter in marriage to the thistle's son—but the thistle was trampled by a wild beast. Amaziah ignored the warning. At Beth-Shemesh, Judah suffered a crushing defeat. Amaziah was captured, part of Jerusalem's wall was torn down for 400 cubits, and the treasures of the temple and palace were plundered.

keyEvents.title: Conspiracy and death in Lachish
keyEvents.description: A conspiracy was formed against Amaziah in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But the conspirators sent men after him, and he was killed there. He was brought back and buried in the City of David. His son Azariah (Uzziah) became king after him.

versions.summary: Amaziah reigned over Judah for 29 years and did what was right in the Lord's eyes, though not with a whole heart. He is known for his victory over the Edomites, but also for his foolishness in challenging King Joash of Israel, which led to a humiliating defeat and the plundering of Jerusalem.
versions.title: The king of Judah who defeated Edom
versions.reason: [major] The lifespan 'ca. 825-796 BC' is problematic. Amaziah reigned for 29 years, and his reign is usually dated to approximately 796-767 BC (or similar dates). The death year of 796 BC does not align with a 29-year reign period. A more reasonable estimate would be ca. 825-767 BC if counting from birth to death, or one could specify the reign period as approximately 796-767 BC; [major] Several of the keyEvents refer to bookId 14 (2 Chronicles), which is correct for the account in the Books of Chronicles. However, the events 'Victory over Edom' and 'Worship of Edomite gods' should also include references from 2 Kings (bookId 12) chapter 14, which provides the parallel account. In particular, 2 Chron 25:11-12 and 2 Kgs 14:7 use different details.; [minor] The event 'Worship of Edomite gods' refers to 2 Chron 25:14-16, but this is found only in the Books of Chronicles, not in the Books of Kings. The reference is correct, but it should be noted that this is unique to the Chronicler's account.; [minor] The defeat against Joash is described in both 2 Chron 25:17-24 and 2 Kgs 14:8-14. Including the parallel reference from 2 Kings (bookId 12, chapter 14) would strengthen the profile.; [minor] The conspiracy and death are also described in 2 Kgs 14:19-20 (bookId 12). A parallel reference should be included.; [minor] The summary is good but could mention that Amaziah worshiped Edomite gods after his victory, which is an important part of his theological profile and the reason for his downfall according to the Chronicler.; [minor] The role 'idolater' or a more neutral description such as 'apostate' could be considered, since his worship of Edomite gods is a central feature of his account.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. A profile of this type should include footnotes on historical, archaeological, or theological aspects.

versions.summary: Amaziah was the son of Joash and reigned as king over Judah for 29 years (about 796–767 B.C.). He did what was right in the Lord's eyes, but not with a whole heart. He punished his father's murderers according to the Law of Moses, and won a great victory over the Edomites in the Valley of Salt. After this victory, however, he brought back the gods of the Edomites and worshiped them, which aroused the Lord's anger. In pride, he then challenged Joash king of Israel to war, but suffered a humiliating defeat at Beth-Shemesh. Jerusalem was plundered and the temple wall was torn down. Eventually a conspiracy was plotted against him, and he was killed in Lachish. His son Azariah (Uzziah) succeeded him as king.
versions.title: King of Judah who defeated Edom but fell into pride
versions.reason: [minor] The lifespan of approximately 825–767 BC is reasonable, but the birth year is uncertain. Some chronologies place his birth somewhat later (around 820 BC). Since he became king at age 25 and began to reign around 796 BC, about 821 BC fits better as a birth year. However, all dating in this period is disputed, so "approximately" is appropriate.; [major] His father Joash (son of Ahaziah) is listed with the ID 'joas-ahasjas-sonn'. This is correct according to 2 Kings 14:1 and 2 Chronicles 25:1. However, it should be verified that this ID actually exists in the database.; [minor] For the victory over Edom in 2 Chronicles, only verses 11–12 are listed, but verses 5–10 provide important context regarding the mustering of the army and the rejection of the hired Israelite soldiers. Consider including more verses for a more complete picture.; [minor] The footnote's classification as "rabbinic" is debatable. The comparison with Jotham's fable and the identification of wisdom literature genre are more literary/linguistic observations than specifically rabbinic tradition. Consider changing the source to "linguistic".; [minor] Amaziah also exercised judicial authority (punishing murderers according to the Mosaic Law). The role "judge" or "law enforcer" could be considered, but "king" covers this implicitly.; [minor] The summary is good and comprehensive, but it could mention that Amaziah also hired and then rejected Israelite mercenaries before the Edom campaign (2 Chronicles 25:5–10), which led to Israeli raids on Judean cities—an important context for the later conflict with Israel.

versions.summary: Amaziah, son of King Joash and Joadan from Jerusalem, reigned as king over Judah for 29 years (approx. 796–767 B.C.). He began his reign at age twenty-five and did what was right in the Lord's sight, but not with a whole heart. He executed the servants who had murdered his father, yet spared their children in accordance with the Law of Moses. Before the campaign against Edom, he hired Israelite soldiers, but sent them home after a prophet's warning – an act that led to Israelite raiding parties against Judah's cities. Amaziah then won a great victory over the Edomites in the Valley of Salt and captured the city of Sela. But following this triumph, he brought back the gods of Edom and worshiped them, which aroused the Lord's anger. Puffed up by his success, he challenged Joash king of Israel to war, but ignored Joash's warning parable about the thornbush and the cedar. At Beth-Shemesh Judah suffered a crushing defeat: Amaziah was taken captive, Jerusalem's wall was torn down, and the temple was plundered. Finally, a conspiracy was plotted against him in Jerusalem, and he was killed while fleeing to Lachish. His son Azariah, also known as Uzziah, succeeded him on the throne.
versions.title: King of Judah who defeated Edom but fell into pride
versions.reason: [minor] In 2 Kings 14:7 it is described that Amaziah struck down ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, but 2 Chronicles 25:11-12 mentions that ten thousand were killed and ten thousand taken alive as prisoners and thrown off a cliff. The description in keyEvents covers only the ten thousand killed from 2 Chronicles 25:11, but omits the ten thousand war captives from verse 12 who were thrown off the cliff. Verse 12 is included in the references, so the description should correspond.; [minor] The fable of the thornbush is rendered imprecisely. In 2 Kings 14:9 and 2 Chronicles 25:18 the fable concerns a thistle (thornbush) on Lebanon that sends a message to the cedar on Lebanon asking to give his daughter to his son – and then a wild beast came and trampled down the thistle. The phrasing 'the thornbush that wanted to court the cedar's daughter' is slightly imprecise; it is the thistle that sends a message to the cedar to give the daughter to the thistle's son.; [minor] The summary is very good and detailed, but the phrasing 'fable of the thornbush and the cedar' could have been more precise as 'fable of the thistle and the cedar' to correspond better with the Hebrew text (חוֹחַ, choach = thistle/thornbush).; [minor] Amaziah's wife is not explicitly named in the biblical text (only his mother Jehoaddan is mentioned), so zero is acceptable, but it could have been useful to note that his wife is unknown.; [minor] 'Warrior' is acceptable, but 'commander' or 'military leader' could have been more precise for a king who led military campaigns. Alternatively, it could be considered adding 'idolater' given the central role his apostasy plays in the biblical account.

footnotes.text: The name Amaziah (Hebrew: אֲמַצְיָהוּ, Amatsyahu) means 'the Lord is strong' or 'strengthened by the Lord.' The full form with the theophoric element -yahu emphasizes the Yahwistic naming tradition among the kings of Judah, making his later worship of foreign gods all the more remarkable.

The Valley of Salt (Hebrew: גֵּיא הַמֶּלַח), where Amaziah defeated the Edomites, is usually identified with Wadi el-Milh south of the Dead Sea. The area was strategically important for controlling trade routes between Eilat, the Red Sea, and the Arabian Peninsula.

The city of Sela, which Amaziah captured (2 Kings 14:7), is traditionally identified with Petra in present-day Jordan, or possibly es-Sela near Bozrah. The Hebrew word sela means 'rock,' which fits well with Petra's topography. Amaziah gave the city a new name: Joktheel.

The Chronicler's account of Amaziah's worship of Edomite gods (2 Chronicles 25:14–16) is not found in the Books of Kings. This is an example of the Chronicler's theological editing, where military pride and religious apostasy are directly linked as explanations for a king's downfall—a recurring pattern in the Chronicler's portrayal of the kings of Judah.

The fable of the thistle and the cedar that Joash used to warn Amaziah (2 Kings 14:9; 2 Chronicles 25:18) belongs to a genre of political fables in the Old Testament (cf. Jotham's fable in Judges 9:7–15). The Hebrew word חוֹחַ (choach) refers to a thistle or thorny plant, and the image of the small thistle haughtily challenging the mighty cedar is a striking political metaphor.

Beth-Shemesh, where the decisive battle between Judah and Israel took place, is identified with Tell er-Rumeileh in the Sorek Valley, about 24 km west of Jerusalem. Archaeological excavations have revealed extensive Iron Age settlement, including storage buildings and fortifications that testify to the city's strategic importance.

Amaziah's rejection of the Israelite mercenaries before the campaign against Edom (2 Chron 25:5–10), following a prophet's warning, led to those dismissed soldiers plundering cities in Judah. This episode illustrates the tension between the two kingdoms and may have contributed to the hostile relationship that culminated in the war at Beth-Shemesh.

According to rabbinic tradition (Sanhedrin 103b), Amaziah is counted among the kings who will not share in the world to come, precisely because of his idolatry after the victory over Edom. The rabbis viewed his downfall as a warning example of how military success can lead to spiritual pride.
